definition:
Atonement is the Bible's answer to the question of how sinful people and a holy God can be brought back together. The English word was formed in the early sixteenth century from the phrase ‘at one’, meaning reconciliation, and William Tyndale's Bible translations helped fix it in English. In Christian teaching it names what God has done in the death of Jesus Christ to deal with sin, to remove the guilt, defilement, and bondage that sin brings, and so to make sinners one with him again. The Old Testament teaches through Israel's sacrifices that sin is deadly serious, that it pollutes and separates, and that God himself provides the means by which it is covered and removed: “I have given it to you to make atonement for your souls upon the altar” (Leviticus 17:11). The New Testament presents the death of Jesus as the sacrifice those offerings pointed toward, and describes it with several pictures at once: a sacrifice for sin, a substitute who bears what others deserved, a ransom that sets captives free, a victory over the powers of evil, and a reconciliation of enemies. The church has never chosen one picture and discarded the rest.

The Hebrew verb is kipper, used around a hundred times, mostly in Leviticus and Numbers, usually rendered ‘make atonement’. Its origin is debated: some connect it to a root meaning ‘to cover’, others to an Akkadian word meaning ‘to wipe off’ or ‘purge’, and others to the noun kopher, ‘ransom’, the price paid to spare a forfeited life (Exodus 30:12). Scholars such as Jay Sklar have argued that in Leviticus it joins the ideas of ransom and cleansing, but its meaning is settled by how it is used, not by its root. Related words are kapporet, the gold lid of the ark of the covenant, rendered ‘mercy seat’ or ‘atonement cover’ (Exodus 25:22), and Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement. In Greek the key words are hilaskomai (‘to make atonement’ or ‘be merciful’, Hebrews 2:17), hilastērion (the Septuagint's word for the mercy seat, used of Christ in Romans 3:25 and of the lid of the ark in Hebrews 9:5), and hilasmos (1 John 2:2; 4:10). Around them stand lytron, ‘ransom’ (Mark 10:45), apolytrōsis, ‘redemption’ (Romans 3:24), and katallassō, ‘to reconcile’ (2 Corinthians 5:18-20).
ot:
Sacrifice appears in Genesis before it is regulated. Abel brings the firstborn of his flock and God looks with favor on him and his offering (Genesis 4:4); Noah builds an altar after the flood (Genesis 8:20); and when God tests Abraham by commanding him to offer Isaac, Abraham tells his son, “God Himself will provide the lamb for the burnt offering” (Genesis 22:8). A ram caught in a thicket is offered “in place of his son” (Genesis 22:13), and the place is named The LORD Will Provide. The chapter does not yet speak of atonement, but it establishes two patterns the rest of Scripture develops: a life given in place of another, and a sacrifice God himself supplies. At the exodus, the blood of the Passover lamb on Israel's doorposts turns aside the judgment on Egypt's firstborn, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13), and at Sinai the covenant is sealed when Moses sprinkles the people with “the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8). After the golden calf Moses goes back up the mountain saying, “perhaps I can make atonement for your sin” (Exodus 32:30), and offers to be blotted out himself, an offer God does not accept.

Leviticus gives the system in detail. Its offerings include the burnt offering, wholly consumed on the altar; the grain offering; the peace or fellowship offering, partly eaten in a shared meal; the sin offering (Hebrew chatta't, which Jacob Milgrom argued is better called a purification offering, since it cleanses the sanctuary); and the guilt or reparation offering ('asham), which accompanies restitution. The worshiper lays a hand on the animal's head “so it can be accepted on his behalf to make atonement for him” (Leviticus 1:4); interpreters differ on whether the gesture signifies ownership, identification, or the transfer of sin. The offerings covered unintentional sins and ritual impurity; for deliberate, defiant sin the law provides no sacrifice (Numbers 15:30-31), though repentance and confession opened the way to mercy. Leviticus 17:11 gives the rationale: “the life of the flesh is in the blood”, and God has given the blood on the altar to make atonement. Sacrifice is not a bribe offered by human beings to a reluctant deity but a gift God appoints so that he can live among a sinful people without consuming them.

The Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), held once a year, is the high point. The high priest alone enters the Most Holy Place behind the veil, where God appears above the mercy seat (Leviticus 16:2). He offers a bull for himself and a goat for the people and sprinkles their blood on and before the mercy seat to “make atonement for the Most Holy Place because of the impurities and rebellious acts of the Israelites” (Leviticus 16:16). A second goat, chosen by lot “for Azazel”, is not killed; the priest lays both hands on it, confesses over it all the iniquities of Israel, and sends it into the wilderness, so that it “will carry on itself all their iniquities into a solitary place” (Leviticus 16:22). Tyndale coined the English word ‘scapegoat’ for it. What Azazel means is disputed: a wilderness demon (as in the later book of 1 Enoch), a remote place, or a term meaning ‘complete removal’. Either way, the day pictures sin both cleansed by blood and carried far away. The chapter ends with the promise, “on this day atonement will be made for you to cleanse you” (Leviticus 16:30).

The Psalms and the Prophets press two further truths. First, sacrifice without a changed heart is worthless. “For I desire mercy, not sacrifice” (Hosea 6:6); “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit” (Psalm 51:17); Micah asks whether God wants thousands of rams or a firstborn child and answers that he requires justice, mercy, and humility (Micah 6:6-8). These texts do not abolish the altar, which Psalm 51 itself expects to be restored (Psalm 51:19), but they refuse to let ritual replace repentance. Second, the sacrifices themselves could not finally be the answer. “No man can possibly redeem his brother or pay his ransom to God” (Psalm 49:7). Into that gap Isaiah's fourth Servant Song (Isaiah 52:13 to 53:12) speaks of a person, not an animal, who suffers for others: “He was pierced for our transgressions, He was crushed for our iniquities; the punishment that brought us peace was upon Him” (Isaiah 53:5). The LORD lays on him the iniquity of all; his life is made a guilt offering, the 'asham of Leviticus (Isaiah 53:10); and he “bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors” (Isaiah 53:12). Jewish interpreters from the Middle Ages onward, Rashi among them, have commonly read the Servant as Israel suffering among the nations, while the New Testament and the church read the passage as fulfilled in Jesus. Daniel 9:24 looks toward a time appointed “to make atonement for iniquity” and bring in everlasting righteousness.
nt:
Jesus spoke of his coming death as necessary and purposeful. He said the Son of Man came “to give His life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45), the lytron language of a life paid for lives, with echoes of the Servant who bore the sin of many. At the Last Supper, a Passover meal, he took the cup and said, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many” (Mark 14:24), joining the covenant blood of Exodus 24:8 to the Servant who poured out his life; Matthew adds “for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28). On the cross he cried the opening words of Psalm 22, asking why God had forsaken him (Mark 15:34). After his resurrection he taught that the Christ had to suffer and so enter his glory (Luke 24:26). John the Baptist calls him “the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world” (John 1:29), a title that gathers the Passover lamb, the lamb of Isaiah 53:7, and perhaps the lamb God provides in Genesis 22. John's Gospel adds that the good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep of his own accord (John 10:11, 18), that Caiaphas unknowingly prophesied that one man would die for the people (John 11:50), and that the cross is where “the prince of this world will be cast out” (John 12:31). John times the crucifixion to the slaughter of the Passover lambs and applies to Jesus the rule that no bone of the lamb be broken (John 19:36).

Paul received as the church's earliest confession “that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures” (1 Corinthians 15:3). In Romans 3:25 God “presented Him as the atoning sacrifice”, using hilastērion, the word for the mercy seat, so that the cross is the place where God deals with sin publicly, demonstrating his justice. Whether hilastērion and its cousins should be rendered ‘propitiation’ (turning away God's wrath) or ‘expiation’ (removing sin) became a twentieth-century debate: C. H. Dodd argued in 1931 for expiation, and Leon Morris in The Apostolic Preaching of the Cross (1955) and Roger Nicole argued that the context of God's wrath (Romans 1:18) requires propitiation. Many scholars now hold that the word includes both, since wrath is removed precisely by removing sin, and that it is God who provides the sacrifice rather than receiving it from us. Paul also speaks of substitution and curse, “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13), and “God made Him who knew no sin to be sin on our behalf” (2 Corinthians 5:21); of redemption “through His blood” (Ephesians 1:7) and a price paid (1 Corinthians 6:20); of reconciliation, in which God, the offended party, takes the initiative: “God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ, not counting men's trespasses against them” (2 Corinthians 5:19); and of victory, in which Christ, “having disarmed the powers and authorities”, made a spectacle of them, “triumphing over them by the cross” (Colossians 2:15). The reconciliation reaches beyond individuals to Jew and Gentile made one body (Ephesians 2:16) and to “all things” in heaven and on earth (Colossians 1:20). Above all, Paul insists that the cross is the Father's love, not its opposite: “God proves His love for us in this: While we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

Hebrews reads the whole Levitical system as a shadow now fulfilled. Christ had to be made like his brothers “in order to make atonement for the sins of the people” (Hebrews 2:17). He is both high priest and sacrifice; he entered not an earthly sanctuary but heaven itself, “by His own blood, thus securing eternal redemption” (Hebrews 9:12). The old sacrifices had to be repeated because “it is impossible for the blood of bulls and goats to take away sins” (Hebrews 10:4), but Christ “appeared once for all at the end of the ages to do away with sin by the sacrifice of Himself” (Hebrews 9:26) and then sat down, his work finished (Hebrews 10:12). Hebrews also says he destroyed the one who holds the power of death and freed those enslaved by the fear of death (Hebrews 2:14-15), the victory theme again. Peter applies Isaiah 53 directly: “He Himself bore our sins in His body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24), and Christ suffered “once for all, the righteous for the unrighteous, to bring you to God” (1 Peter 3:18). John writes that Christ “is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not only for ours but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2), and defines love by it: “not that we loved God, but that He loved us and sent His Son as the atoning sacrifice for our sins” (1 John 4:10). Revelation ends with the Lamb who was slain standing at the center of the throne, worshiped because “by Your blood You purchased for God those from every tribe and tongue and people and nation” (Revelation 5:9), and with the saints who conquered the accuser “by the blood of the Lamb” (Revelation 12:11).

keyTexts.why: God provides a ram in place of Isaac, and the place is named The LORD Will Provide. The patterns of substitution and of God supplying the sacrifice begin here.
The blood of the Passover lamb shields Israel's firstborn from judgment. The New Testament calls Jesus the Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7).
The Day of Atonement: blood on the mercy seat cleanses the sanctuary, and the second goat carries Israel's sins away. Hebrews reads Christ's work through this chapter.
Life is in the blood, and God has given it on the altar to make atonement. The sacrificial system is God's gift, not a human bribe.
No one can pay the ransom for another's life. The need the Old Testament raises and cannot itself meet.
The suffering Servant is pierced for others' transgressions, makes his life a guilt offering, and bears the sin of many. The Old Testament text the New Testament most often uses for the cross.
Jesus came to give his life as a ransom for many. His own interpretation of his death.
At the Last Supper Jesus speaks of his blood of the covenant poured out for many, joining Sinai and Isaiah 53.
The Lamb of God takes away the sin of the world. A title that gathers Passover, Isaiah 53, and the lamb God provides.
God presented Christ as the hilastērion, the atoning sacrifice, so that he is both just and the one who justifies. The center of the propitiation and expiation debate.
God reconciles the world to himself in Christ, not counting trespasses, and made the sinless one to be sin for us.
The record of debt is cancelled and the powers are disarmed and led in triumph by the cross. The chief text of the victory theme.
Christ, priest and sacrifice at once, enters the true sanctuary by his own blood and secures eternal redemption.
Peter quotes Isaiah 53 of Christ, who bore our sins in his body on the tree, and makes the cross both the ground of healing and the pattern of the Christian life.
Love is defined by God sending his Son as the atoning sacrifice. The cross is the Father's love, not a price extracted from him.

history:
No ecumenical council ever defined a single theory of the atonement. The Nicene Creed confesses that the Son came down for us and for our salvation and was crucified for us under Pontius Pilate, and the early church preached the cross with the full range of biblical images. Irenaeus of Lyon, writing Against Heresies around 180, taught recapitulation: Christ went back over the whole of human life as a second Adam, obeying where Adam disobeyed, and so undid the fall from within. Athanasius's On the Incarnation (probably in the 320s or 330s) argued that the Word became man so that by his death he could pay the debt of death owed by all and restore God's image in humanity. Origen and later Gregory of Nyssa described the cross as a ransom paid to the devil, who held humanity captive, and Gregory pictured the humanity of Christ as bait concealing the hook of his divinity. Gregory of Nazianzus rejected the idea that any ransom was paid to the devil, and he also denied that the Father required it for his own sake.

The decisive medieval work was Anselm of Canterbury's Cur Deus Homo (Why God Became Man), completed in 1098. Anselm argued that sin dishonors God, that justice requires either punishment or a satisfaction greater than the offense, that only God could make such a satisfaction and only a man ought to, and so the one who makes it must be both. Peter Abelard, in his commentary on Romans (in the 1130s), stressed that Christ's death reveals God's love and kindles love in return; later writers built a moral influence theory on this emphasis, though scholars debate whether Abelard himself held nothing more. Thomas Aquinas (Summa Theologiae III, questions 46 to 49) drew the strands together, treating Christ's passion as merit, satisfaction, sacrifice, and redemption. The Council of Trent's decree on the Mass (1562) taught that the Eucharist is a true sacrifice that re-presents the one sacrifice of the cross, not a new one; Protestants rejected this teaching as compromising the once-for-all offering of Hebrews.

The Reformers kept Anselm's framework but spoke of Christ bearing the penalty of sin, not only rendering satisfaction to God's honor. Luther wrote of a joyous exchange in which Christ takes the believer's sin and gives his righteousness (The Freedom of a Christian, 1520), and Calvin (Institutes 2.16) taught that Christ bore the curse and the penalty of God's judgment in our place. This became known as penal substitution. Faustus Socinus attacked the whole idea of satisfaction in De Jesu Christo Servatore (published 1594), arguing that forgiveness and payment are incompatible; Hugo Grotius's Defense of the Catholic Faith concerning the Satisfaction of Christ (1617) answered him with what came to be called the governmental view. The Synod of Dort (1618-1619) and the later debates over the extent of the atonement, for whom Christ died, are surveyed on the site's page on how we are saved.

In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the question reopened. John McLeod Campbell's The Nature of the Atonement (1856) spoke of Christ's perfect response to the Father on humanity's behalf; Horace Bushnell's The Vicarious Sacrifice (1866) stressed moral influence. Gustaf Aulén's Christus Victor (Swedish 1930, English 1931) argued that the victory theme was the classic view of the church fathers and Luther. C. H. Dodd's 1931 essay and Leon Morris's reply renewed the propitiation question, and John Stott's The Cross of Christ (1986) became a widely read defense of substitution alongside the other images. In the early twenty-first century, Steve Chalke and Alan Mann's The Lost Message of Jesus (2003) sharply criticized penal substitution and Steve Jeffery, Michael Ovey, and Andrew Sach's Pierced for Our Transgressions (2007) defended it. The site's page on how we are saved sets out the related debates.

differ.body: Sin deserves the just judgment of God, and on the cross Christ bore that judgment in the place of sinners. This is not an angry Father punishing an unwilling Son; the triune God himself, in love, takes the penalty into himself in the person of the Son, who lays down his life freely. Defenders, from Calvin to John Stott, point to Isaiah 53:5-6, Galatians 3:13, 2 Corinthians 5:21, 1 Peter 2:24, and the language of wrath and propitiation in Romans 1 to 3. They hold that substitution is the heart that holds the other images together: Christ defeats the powers precisely by removing the guilt that gave them their claim (Colossians 2:14-15), and the cross shows love precisely because it accomplished something for us.

Following Anselm and Thomas Aquinas, and in the main line of Roman Catholic teaching, sin is an offense against God's honor and against the order of justice, and it calls for satisfaction, a reparation offered freely out of love. Christ, as God and man, offers to the Father a perfect obedience and self-offering whose worth far exceeds the offense, and this satisfaction is superabundant because of who he is. The emphasis falls on Christ's loving obedience rather than on punishment as such. Defenders argue that this reading honors the sacrificial language of Hebrews and the Gospels, keeps the Father and Son united in one loving will, and grounds the church's participation in Christ's offering, above all in the Eucharist.

The cross is first of all God's victory over the powers that hold humanity captive: sin, death, and the devil. Defenders, following Gustaf Aulén, argue that this was the dominant note in the church fathers and in Luther, and they point to Genesis 3:15, Colossians 2:15, Hebrews 2:14-15, 1 John 3:8, and Revelation 12:11. God in Christ entered enemy territory, allowed himself to be killed by the powers, and broke them from within by rising. Many holding this view see it as the frame within which substitution and sacrifice make sense; some, including many in the Eastern Orthodox tradition, prefer it to legal categories altogether.

The cross reveals the depth of God's love so powerfully that it breaks human resistance and draws people to repentance and love in return. Associated with Peter Abelard's emphasis and with Horace Bushnell and much nineteenth-century Protestant theology, the view stresses texts like Romans 5:8, John 12:32, and 1 John 4:10. Its defenders hold that God never needed to be changed toward us, only we toward him, and that the other models risk picturing God as bound by a law above him. Critics respond that a death demonstrates love only if it accomplishes something for the one loved, and most who stress this theme today hold it alongside an objective work.

Associated with Hugo Grotius and later with much Arminian and New England theology, this view holds that God, as the just ruler of the moral universe, forgives freely but cannot simply ignore sin without undermining his law and government. The death of Christ is a public demonstration of God's hatred of sin and the seriousness of his law, upholding justice so that God can forgive the repentant. Christ did not pay the exact penalty owed by each person, but his suffering satisfied the requirements of good government. Defenders point to Romans 3:25-26, where the cross demonstrates God's righteousness, and argue that the view preserves both free forgiveness and moral order.

errors:
The church has rejected several distortions of the atonement, even while leaving its models open. The first sets the Father against the Son, as if a loving Son had to persuade a wrathful Father to relent. Scripture insists that the Father sent the Son in love (John 3:16; 1 John 4:10), that “God was reconciling the world to Himself in Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:19), and that the Son laid down his life freely (John 10:18). The persons of the Trinity act together in every work of God, and every orthodox account of the cross has to honor that. The second treats sacrifice as a bribe offered by human beings to win over a reluctant deity, the logic of pagan appeasement; in Leviticus it is God who gives the blood for atonement (Leviticus 17:11), and in the New Testament it is God who presents the sacrifice (Romans 3:25). The third, taught by Faustus Socinus and in much later liberal theology, reduces the cross to an example of faithfulness or love with no work accomplished for us; the historic confessions, Catholic, Orthodox, and Protestant, all teach that Christ's death did something objective that we could not do. The fourth, drawn from pressing the ransom picture too far, imagines that the devil had legal rights over humanity that God had to buy off; Gregory of Nazianzus and Anselm both rejected it.

Two further errors concern the finality of the cross. Hebrews insists the sacrifice was offered once for all and cannot be repeated or added to (Hebrews 9:26; 10:14). Catholics and Protestants agree on that principle while disagreeing about how the Eucharist relates to the one sacrifice. And the atonement is distorted when it is treated as mere private transaction with no call to a changed life, when Peter says Christ bore our sins “so that we might die to sin and live to righteousness” (1 Peter 2:24).
life:
The atonement tells a person two things at once. It tells the truth about sin: that it is not a small matter, a mistake to be shrugged off or a bad habit to be managed, but something that cost the life of the Son of God. And it tells the truth about God's love: that he did not wait for sinners to make things right but came himself, while we were still enemies, and paid the cost. The first keeps confession honest; the second keeps it from despair. A person who has looked at the cross cannot pretend his sin is nothing, and cannot believe it is too great to forgive.

The cross also shapes how Christians live with one another and with suffering. Peter tells slaves who suffer unjustly that Christ left them an example, and the whole New Testament calls believers to forgive as they were forgiven, to lay down their lives for one another (1 John 3:16), and to be agents of the reconciliation they received (2 Corinthians 5:18-20). It shapes worship too: the Lord's Supper places the broken body and poured-out blood at the center of the church's life every time it gathers. And it gives hope in the face of death and evil, because the powers that seem strongest were disarmed at the place where they seemed to win.
questions: Leviticus 17:11 says God gave the blood on the altar to make atonement. How does that change the picture of sacrifice as something people do to win God over?

The New Testament describes the cross as sacrifice, substitution, ransom, victory, and reconciliation. Which of these pictures do you find most natural, which most difficult, and what would be lost if one were dropped?
Romans 5:8 and 1 John 4:10 say the cross proves God's love. How would you answer someone who hears the doctrine of the atonement as a story of an angry Father and a victim Son?
